# Cubic cap-band double-gain barrier and an actual two-ceiling obstruction

This note proves a finite raw-data barrier for the cubic PSD inequality.
Its exact counterexample shows why two captured-cap ceilings alone cannot
replace the full band in that barrier. The counterexample is an actual
triangle; its tested pure-gain direction is expressly NOT geometrically
feasible with fixed cutting chords.

## 1. Raw functional and its derivatives

For positive total area k, cap areas Q_i and coarea chord lengths sigma_i,
put

    M=sum_i Q_i/sigma_i,
    f_i=2 sqrt(k Q_i)/(sigma_i M),
    Psi=sum_i f_i^2+f_1 f_2 f_3.

In particular sum_i f_i sqrt(Q_i/k)=2. Fix all sigma_i. At a positive
boundary point Psi=4 write

    P=f_1 f_2 f_3, E_i=2f_i^2+P, C=sum_i E_i=8+P.

Increasing k,Q_j,Q_l by the same amount while holding the omitted Q_s
fixed is the exact raw change from adding area to the double sector
missed by cap s. Its Psi derivative beta_s satisfies

    2k beta_s=C+sum_(i != s)[E_i T_i^2-C f_i T_i],
    T_i=sqrt(k/Q_i).                                      (1)

This follows by logarithmic differentiation of f_i. The unique-loss
derivative, when k and Q_s decrease together, is the negative of alpha_s,
where

    2k alpha_s=C+E_s T_s^2-C f_s T_s
       >=C P(4-f_s^2)/(4E_s)>0.                          (2)

The completed-square proof of (2) is in
`candidate b59c030c1c2567d0`.

## 2. Exact negative double-gain derivative throughout the cap band

Assume every Q_i/k is at most c=128/279. Let s_c=sqrt(c) and F=sum f_i.
The cubic boundary implies all three Lorentz rows, and hence F<=3.
The moment identity gives

    F>=2/s_c>59/20,                                     (3)

because 128/279<(40/59)^2. At fixed F each Lorentz inequality is

    [f_i-(F-2)]^2<=4(3-F).

Writing delta=3-F in [0,1/20), these inequalities give

    1/2<f_i<3/2.                                       (4)

For the lower bound, f_i>=1-delta-2sqrt(delta)>
19/20-1/sqrt(5)>1/2; the upper bound follows from
f_i<=1+2sqrt(delta)<1+1/sqrt(5)<3/2.

The moment identity, the ceiling, and F<=3 further give, for each i,

    2<=f_i sqrt(Q_i/k)+(3-f_i)s_c,
    sqrt(Q_i/k)>=s_c-(3s_c-2)/f_i>4-5s_c>3/5.

Here s_c<17/25 and 3s_c-2>0. Also sqrt(Q_i/k)<=s_c<7/10.
Consequently

    10/7<T_i<5/3.                                     (5)

At the cubic boundary, P<=1: indeed sum f_i^2>=3P^(2/3),
and 3P^(2/3)+P<=4 implies P<=1. Thus 8<C<=9.

Fix the omitted index s and abbreviate

    x=f_s, S=f_j+f_l, D=f_j-f_l.

Then S=F-x, |D|<1, and

    E_j+E_l=8-2x^2=2(4-x^2),
    E_j-E_l=2S D.                                     (6)

The right side of (1) is separately convex in T_j,T_l. It is enough
to check their four closed endpoint choices from (5).

If both equal t, where t is 10/7 or 5/3, the expression is

    C(1-tS)+2t^2(4-x^2).

Since S>29/20, we have 1-tS<0. Using C>=8, S>=59/20-x,
and completing the square in x gives the upper bound

    8[2-(59/20)t+t^2].                                 (7)

Its values are -68/49 and -10/9, respectively.

For mixed endpoints put t=65/42 and e=5/42. The expression in (1) is

    C(1-tS)+2(t^2+e^2)(4-x^2)
                       +/- eD(4tS-C).                 (8)

As before its first two terms, omitting the e^2 term, are bounded by
8[2-(59/20)t+t^2]. The extra e^2 term is at most 8e^2.
From 29/20<S<5/2 and 8<C<=9,

    |4tS-C|<=10t-8.

For clarity the lower endpoint gives 4tS-C>29t/5-9=-1/42,
whereas 10t-8=157/21>1/42. Since |D|<1, (8) is at most

    8[2-(59/20)t+t^2]+8e^2+e(10t-8)
       =-317/882<0.                                   (9)

Equations (7)--(9) prove beta_s<0 for every omitted index. This is an
explicit cubic derivative certificate, not a deduction from separate
Lorentz derivative signs.

## 3. Finite combined barrier

Start with positive k,Q_i,sigma_i, with Psi<=4 and all cap fractions at
most c. Prescribe nonnegative unique-sector losses E_i and double-sector
gains G_i, with E=sum E_i and G=sum G_i. Keep all sigma_i fixed and set

    k(t)=k+t(G-E),
    Q_i(t)=Q_i+t(G-G_i-E_i),       0<=t<=1.

Suppose the endpoint data are positive and the final cap fractions are
also at most c. Every intermediate k,Q_i is positive. Each ratio Q_i/k
is fractional linear with derivative of constant sign, and hence stays
in the band between its endpoint values. At every Psi=4 contact,

    Psi'(t)=-sum_i E_i alpha_i+sum_i G_i beta_i<0

if any change is nonzero, by (2) and Section 2. The usual first-contact
argument therefore proves final Psi<=4, strictly if there was a nonzero
change. No actual realization of intermediate data is required for this
analytic statement. Applications to convex bodies must separately retain
the actual interpretation of their fixed sections and sector changes.

## 4. Two captured-cap ceilings do not suffice, even at triangle data

Take the actual triangle with vertices

    P_1=(87/100,-49/100),
    P_2=(-1/200,1/100),
    P_3=(-1/200,-23/200),

and the canonical normals e_1,e_2,-e_1-e_2 at zero. Its signed column
matrix has positive diagonal (87/100,1/100,3/25), with negative rows

    row 1: b_12=b_13=1/200,
    row 2: b_21=49/100, b_23=23/200,
    row 3: b_31=19/50, b_32=1/200.

Every column sums to zero. Its positive principal cofactors show that
zero is interior, as in the exact signed-triangle construction. Each
normal strictly isolates its corresponding vertex. The exact triangle
cap and section formulas give

    f=(7/4,1/2,1/2),
    (Q_1/k,Q_2/k,Q_3/k)
       =((174/175)^2,(1/25)^2,(12/25)^2).

Both cap 2 and cap 3 fractions are less than 128/279, and Psi=4.
For a hypothetical pure double-sector gain omitted by cap 1,

    C=135/16,
    2k beta_1=371855/768>0.                            (10)

Thus the sign conclusion in Section 2 fails if its full cap ceiling is
replaced by ceilings on just the two captured caps. This is not a convex
body counterexample to the cubic: at a triangle, pure fixed-chord double
growth is infeasible. The exact PSD matrix has singular unique-corner
blocks and such a gain makes a kernel test negative. The two neighboring
unique losses and their full Schur-complement cost must be retained.
